newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Savings scam forces more Albanians across border.
newsitem.headline: Savings scam forces more Albanians across border.

text.p: Albanians are flooding out of the country illegally in increasing numbers following an investment scheme scandal which left thousands destitute, causing major concern in neighbouring states.

Scores of people can be seen every day walking towards Albania's southern border with Greece, while others crowd into the border town of Gjirokaster, ready to pay up to $550 to fixers who will help smuggle them across the frontier, local residents say.

Meanwhile, hundreds of Albanians queue daily at the Greek embassy in Tirana and the Greek consulate in Gjirokaster, applying for visas to work in Greece after losing their life savings when five high-yield, high-risk investment schemes collapsed last month, sparking protests across the country.
"I invested my savings from a year and a half's work in Greece but...I could not receive the 280,000 leks (about $2,800) I put into the schemes," Ardian, from the northern town of Lezhe, said.
Hundreds of thousands of people in Europe's poorest state of 3.4 million have lost their savings in pyramid investment schemes which proliferated after the fall of the harsh Stalinist regime in 1990.
Ardian and a dozen others from his town, two of them 55 years old, said they would cross the border on foot.
"We know we'll have to live rough in a foreign country but we can earn money and then I could start a business in Lezhe," he said.

One man who helps smuggle would-be immigrants into Greece said they either handed out forged travel documents or accompanied them just over the border before handing them on to Greek taxi drivers who would ferry them to a city.
"The number of people coming with the aim of crossing the border has almost doubled compared to last year," he said.
"Many people walk for as much as 20 days as they don't have money to pay," he said.
Small hotel owners in Gjirokaster said many more people from around the country were arriving in the town before crossing into Greece.
"We've seen a significant rise this year," one hotel proprietor said.

Greece has been swamped by illegal Albanian workers since 1990, when 45 years of hard Stalinist rule ended. An estimated 350,000 Albanians currently live in Greece, usually carrying out the most menial jobs.
Greek authorities have been bracing for another influx of illegal immigrants since the investment scheme scam hit home.

"I have gone to Greece 25 times in the last fours years and was turned back by Greek police each time after a short stay," said Luan, a 32-year-old father of three from the northern district of Diber. "This is my way of living, I cannot work anywhere here in Albania."
